Indicate the number of students: • enrolled in school. • formally screened in the absence of known risk factors. • identified as being at-risk or already experiencing a mental health problem. • referred to a mental health services following identification. Document how many students were screened for each specific screening area: depression, suicidality, substance use, trauma, and other mental health concerns (e.g., ADHD, conduct, life satisfaction, academic engagement). Tips Start small: Many schools and districts have found that piloting screening procedures with small groups of students is helpful to best understand and adapt screening procedures. Starting small and scaling up to the entire student population in a gradual way allows school and district teams to make course corrections and build on successes. pooled.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 6 injury, and possibly suicide (Pedrelli el al., 2015). Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified. Clinical Question In college-aged students (P), how does screening for depression with the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) (I) compared to current practice (C) affect early identification of depression (O)?

pooled.text: that feelings of belonging have in the success and wellness of adoles- cents and young adults. Research has begun to investigate the role that social factors play in the development of depression. Previous research has identified social stressors (e.g., relation- ship breakup) as risk factors for depression (Kendler et al., 1999, 2003; Monroe et al., 1999). Similarly, loneli- ness is associated with higher rates of depression, par - ticularly in young adults (Cacioppo et al., 2006, 2010; Matthews et al., 2016). Initial cross-sectional work has also identified lack of belonging as a predictor of depressive symptoms (Parr et al., 2020). Many self-report assessments of depressive symptoms include questions that assess social functioning; for example, the Center for Epidemiological Studies-Depression (CES-D) scale asks participants to rate social-functioning statements such as “I talked less than usual,” “People were unfriendly,” “I felt that people dislike me,” and “I felt lonely” (Lewinsohn et al., 1997), suggesting that depres- sive symptoms overlap with social experiences as well. The relationship between social factors and depression in young adults specifically has important implications as well. College students often have access to mental health treatment on campus, but the majority with mood disorders do not seek treatment (Blanco et al., 2008). When left untreated, depression in university students can have serious negative consequences on academic performance (Hysenbegasi et al., 2005) and physical health (Dalton & Hammen, 2018) and can lead to suicidal ideation (Beck et al., 1993; Garlow et al., 2008).
